Let the eigenvalues of the real symmetric matrix \(M\) be \(x,y,z\). Since
\[
\operatorname{tr}(M^2)=x^2+y^2+z^2,\qquad \det M=xyz,
\]
Weyl’s integration formula gives
\[
I_n=K\int_{\mathbb R^3}
e^{-n((xyz)^2+(x^2+y^2+z^2)^4)}
|(x-y)(x-z)(y-z)|\,dx\,dy\,dz,
\]
with \(K=\pi^2/3\).

Put \(x=n^{-1/8}X\), \(y=n^{-1/8}Y\), \(z=n^{-1/8}Z\), and \(\mu=n^{1/4}\). Then
\[
I_n=K n^{-3/4}J(\mu),
\]
where
\[
J(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-(X^2+Y^2+Z^2)^4-\mu X^2Y^2Z^2}
|(X-Y)(X-Z)(Y-Z)|\,dX\,dY\,dZ.
\]

As \(\mu\to\infty\), the main contribution comes from one eigenvalue near \(0\). For example, near \(Z=0\), set \(Z=\mu^{-1/2}W\). Summing over the three coordinate planes gives
\[
J(\mu)=\mu^{-1/2}\frac{3\sqrt{2\pi}}2\Gamma(3/8)+O(\mu^{-3/4}).
\]
Thus the leading term is exactly
\[
K n^{-3/4}\mu^{-1/2}\frac{3\sqrt{2\pi}}2\Gamma(3/8)
=\frac{\pi^{5/2}\Gamma(3/8)}{\sqrt2\,n^{7/8}}.
\]

The next contribution comes from the pairwise intersections of those planes, i.e. from rank-one matrices. Near, say, \(Y=Z=0\), set
\[
X=t,\qquad Y=\mu^{-1/4}p,\qquad Z=\mu^{-1/4}q.
\]
After subtracting the already-counted one-plane terms, the finite transverse constant is
\[
B=\lim_{R\to\infty}\left(
\int_{[-R,R]^2}|p-q|e^{-p^2q^2}\,dp\,dq-4R\sqrt\pi
\right).
\]
Splitting into same-sign and opposite-sign quadrants gives
\[
B=-4\Gamma(3/4).
\]
Therefore the rank-one contribution to \(J(\mu)\), summed over the three choices of the large eigenvalue, is
\[
3\mu^{-3/4}\left(\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-t^8}|t|^{1/2}\,dt\right)B
=
3\mu^{-3/4}\left(\frac14\Gamma(3/16)\right)(-4\Gamma(3/4)).
\]
So
\[
J(\mu)=\mu^{-1/2}\frac{3\sqrt{2\pi}}2\Gamma(3/8)
-3\Gamma(3/4)\Gamma(3/16)\mu^{-3/4}
+o(\mu^{-3/4}).
\]
Since \(n^{-3/4}\mu^{-3/4}=n^{-15/16}\), the desired limit is
\[
K\bigl(-3\Gamma(3/4)\Gamma(3/16)\bigr)
=
-\pi^2\Gamma(3/4)\Gamma(3/16).
\]

\[
\boxed{-\pi^2\Gamma(3/4)\Gamma(3/16)}
\]
